lesson.title: Scaling a Limit: The Constant Multiple Rule
lesson.summary: The constant multiple rule says that multiplying a function by a fixed number before taking a limit is the same as taking the limit first and then multiplying by that number.
lesson.body:
Scaling a function by a constant is one of the gentlest operations you can perform on it, and limits respond to it just as gently. If f(x) is closing in on a value L as x approaches a, then stretching or shrinking every output of f by a fixed factor c simply stretches or shrinks the target value by the same factor. Nothing about the underlying approach behavior changes, only the scale on which it is measured.

The Constant Multiple Rule for Limits states that if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals L, then for any real number c, the limit of c times f(x) as x approaches a equals c times L. As noted in the discussion of the product rule, this is really a special case of that rule: think of c as a constant function g(x) equal to c for every x, whose limit at any point is trivially c, since it never varies. Plugging that into the product rule immediately gives the constant multiple rule as a corollary, though it is useful enough to name and use on its own.

Consider this worked example. Let f(x) equal x squared plus 2x, and evaluate the limit of 5 times f(x) as x approaches 3. First find the limit of f(x) alone: 3 squared plus 2 times 3 equals 9 plus 6, which is 15. By the constant multiple rule, the limit of 5 times f(x) is 5 times 15, which equals 75. Checking directly against the combined expression, 5 times (x squared plus 2x) evaluated at x equals 3 gives 5 times (9 plus 6), which is 5 times 15, again 75. The two approaches agree.

Beyond individual computations, the constant multiple rule is what justifies pulling constants outside a limit expression before doing any other work, which very often simplifies the algebra that follows. It also combines neatly with the sum rule to produce the difference rule from first principles: the limit of f(x) minus g(x) can be rewritten as the limit of f(x) plus negative 1 times g(x), which by the sum rule equals the limit of f(x) plus the limit of negative 1 times g(x), and by the constant multiple rule with c equal to negative 1, that second piece equals negative 1 times the limit of g(x). Putting the pieces back together gives L minus M, exactly the difference rule, built entirely out of the sum rule and the constant multiple rule rather than needing to be proven separately.

This kind of layering, where one limit law falls out as a direct consequence of two simpler ones, is a preview of how the whole family of limit laws fits together: sum, product, constant multiple, and the power rule that comes next all interact consistently, so you rarely need to memorize more than a couple of them from scratch.

The constant multiple rule also explains a habit many students develop naturally without ever naming it: pulling a constant out to the front of a limit expression before doing any other simplification. If you are asked for the limit of 10 times (x squared minus 4) divided by (x minus 2) as x approaches 2, it is legitimate to rewrite this as 10 times the limit of (x squared minus 4) divided by (x minus 2), handle the more complicated rational part on its own using whatever technique it needs, and multiply the constant back in only at the very end. That separation keeps the arithmetic simpler at every step and is justified entirely by the constant multiple rule.
